questions.question: 1. What does the push operation on a stack do?

answers.a: Adds an element to the bottom of the stack.
answers.b: Adds an element to the top of the stack.
answers.c: Removes an element from the top of the stack.
answers.d: Adds an element in the middle of the stack.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Push does not place a new element at the bottom of a stack.
explanations.b: Correct. Push inserts a new element at the top of the stack.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Removing an element from the top is the pop operation.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A standard stack does not insert elements into the middle.

questions.question: 2. Situation: A teacher wants to process the operators in an arithmetic expression while temporarily remembering operators that cannot yet be placed in the output. Which approach best represents the use of a stack?

answers.a: Teacher memorizes all operators without keeping any order.
answers.b: Teacher asks a favorite student to remember all operators and use them whenever needed.
answers.c: Teacher places each pending operator on top of a stack and removes the most recent applicable operator first.
answers.d: Teacher asks every student to remember every operator in the expression.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Simply memorizing the operators does not provide the ordered insertion and removal behavior needed during conversion.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Using one person to remember all operators does not model the stack's last-in, first-out access.
explanations.c: Correct. A stack temporarily stores pending operators so that the most recently stored applicable operator can be removed first.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Remembering every operator independently does not provide the controlled last-in, first-out behavior of a stack.

questions.question: 3. Situation: A teacher wants to process an arithmetic expression using a stack. What is an important limitation of this approach?

answers.a: It eliminates the need to consider operator precedence.
answers.b: Access to an arbitrary item in the stack is not the normal operation; stack access is restricted to the top.
answers.c: It requires all operands to be stored permanently in the stack.
answers.d: It makes every arithmetic expression invalid.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Operator precedence still has to be considered when deciding when operators can be moved to the output.
explanations.b: Correct. A stack is designed for access at its top, so arbitrary middle elements are not directly accessed as in an array.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Operands can be processed according to the conversion procedure; they do not all have to remain permanently in the stack.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Stack-based processing can convert valid arithmetic expressions; it does not make expressions invalid.

questions.question: 4. Which of the following best describes a stack?

answers.a: People standing in a queue at a service counter.
answers.d: A set of dinner plates placed on top of one another.

explanations.a: Incorrect. A service line normally follows first-in, first-out behavior rather than stack behavior.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A family tree represents hierarchical relationships rather than last-in, first-out access.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A football team is a collection of players and does not inherently define stack operations.
explanations.d: Correct. Plates are typically added to and removed from the top, illustrating last-in, first-out behavior.

questions.question: 5. On what principle are objects inserted and removed in stacks?

explanations.a: Correct. A stack follows the Last In, First Out principle: the most recently inserted item is removed first.
explanations.b: Incorrect. FIFO describes queue behavior, where the earliest inserted item is removed first.
explanations.c: Incorrect. LILO is not the standard access principle used by a stack.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A stack has a defined access principle, so this option does not describe it.

questions.question: 6. Which notation places the operator between its operands, as in $a+b$?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Prefix notation places the operator before its operands.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Postfix notation places the operator after its operands.
explanations.c: Correct. Infix notation places the operator between its operands, as in $a+b$.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Reverse Polish notation is another name for postfix notation.

questions.question: 7. Why is operator precedence important when converting an infix expression to postfix?

answers.a: It determines the order in which operators should be placed in the postfix expression.
answers.b: It changes every operand into an operator.
answers.c: It removes all parentheses without considering operator relationships.
answers.d: It determines the variable names used in the expression.

explanations.a: Correct. Operator precedence determines which operators must be processed before lower-precedence operators in the resulting postfix expression.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Operator precedence does not change the roles of operands and operators.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Parentheses are removed from the postfix form, but their grouping information must still be respected during conversion.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Variable names are independent of operator precedence.

questions.question: 8. What is the main purpose of converting a valid infix expression to postfix notation?

answers.a: To make the expression contain more operators.
answers.b: To represent the expression so that evaluation can proceed without relying on infix parentheses and precedence during evaluation.
answers.c: To change every operator into a unary operator.
answers.d: To guarantee that the expression contains only numbers.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Conversion does not add unnecessary operators to an expression.
explanations.b: Correct. Postfix notation places operators after their operands, making the evaluation order explicit without requiring infix-style precedence rules during evaluation.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Conversion does not change the arity of the operators.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Postfix expressions can contain variables as operands as well as numeric operands.

questions.question: 9. For the infix expression $a+b*c$, which relationship between the operators must be respected during conversion?

answers.a: Addition must be performed before multiplication.
answers.b: Multiplication must be placed so that it is evaluated before addition.
answers.c: The operators must always be processed from right to left.
answers.d: Both operators have to be removed from the expression.

explanations.a: Incorrect. The expression's operator hierarchy does not give addition priority over multiplication.
explanations.b: Correct. Multiplication has higher precedence than addition, so the postfix form must preserve multiplication before the addition.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Operator precedence does not mean that all operators are processed from right to left.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Conversion rearranges operator placement but does not remove the operators.
